info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 4.1: Diplomatic Transcription by Hand: Building the Ground Truth.

name.text: 01 Question: Why the Manual Step Comes First

questiontext.text: Why does this week ask you to type the page out by hand before running any software on it?

generalfeedback.text: Today's transcription is the measuring instrument for the rest of the term — every error rate you compute is a distance from it.

answer.text: Because the software's output has to be graded, and grading needs an answer key that somebody checked.

feedback.text: Correct. Without a reference you know to be right, machine output is just text — it might be accurate, and you would have no way to tell.

answer.text: Because the software cannot open manuscript images until a person has tagged the vocabulary first.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These programs take images directly. What they cannot supply is a correct version to be measured against.

answer.text: Because typing by hand is more accurate than any software, so the machine passes are really just a demonstration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand transcription contains errors too — that is why Week 5 types the page a second time. The point is that it is the reference, not that it is perfect.

answer.text: Because it is a traditional skill that students should practise before being allowed to use modern tools.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a structural requirement: every error rate is a distance from a reference, so the reference has to exist first.

name.text: 02 Question: Diplomatic Versus Normalized Transcription

questiontext.text: Why must today's transcription copy the page exactly rather than tidy up the spelling and abbreviations?

generalfeedback.text: Transcribe diplomatically, because a model trained on normalized text learns to silently modernize — and Week 6 needs the unnormalized base.

answer.text: Software learns from the examples you give it, so tidied-up examples teach it to quietly replace what the scribe wrote with modern forms.

feedback.text: Correct. And because the tidied output is clean and readable, nothing signals that the historical record has been overwritten.

answer.text: Copying exactly is quicker, because you can ignore the accents and the odd letter shapes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is slower and more demanding — you have to record every surface feature rather than smoothing them away.

answer.text: TEI does not allow tidied-up spelling to be recorded in a digital edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI has `<reg>` for exactly that. The point is that tidying should be done from a faithful base, with each change recorded — which is Week 6's job.

answer.text: Tidied-up transcriptions cannot be turned into web pages or printed editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are easy to present. The problem is that the evidence has already been destroyed by then.

name.text: 03 Question: One Text, Two Structures

questiontext.text: A sentence starts halfway down a line and finishes on the next page. Why is that a problem for XML, and how does TEI solve it?

generalfeedback.text: Physical and logical structure both exist and do not nest, so TEI records line and page boundaries as empty milestones within the logical hierarchy.

answer.text: XML needs tags to nest neatly, and the page's structure and the text's structure overlap instead — so TEI marks page and line starts with empty tags that mark a point rather than wrapping anything.

feedback.text: Correct. `<pb/>` and `<lb/>` sit inside the paragraph as markers, so the paragraph stays one tidy box.

answer.text: XML cannot represent pages at all, so line and page breaks are recorded in a separate file and linked back.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are recorded inline, in the same file, as empty marker tags.

answer.text: TEI solves it by ending the paragraph at the page break and starting a new one on the next page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would misrepresent the text — one sentence would become two paragraphs. The paragraph continues; only a marker is inserted.

answer.text: It is not really a problem, because scribes almost always ended sentences at the end of a line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They frequently did not, and even a single overlap is enough to break strict nesting.

name.text: 04 Question: The Tags You Will Actually Use

questiontext.text: What does `<choice>` do in a diplomatic transcription?

generalfeedback.text: `<choice>` holds alternatives rather than deciding between them, so one encoding can serve palaeographic, reading, and search views.

answer.text: It holds two versions of the same text side by side, so a computer can pick whichever suits the job later.

feedback.text: Correct. A reading edition shows the spelled-out form, a handwriting study shows the short form, and you only encoded it once.

answer.text: It picks the more likely of two readings and records that one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It deliberately does not choose — that is the whole point of the element.

answer.text: It marks a passage where the scribe had a choice of wording and took one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is about your encoding of the text, not about the scribe's decisions. Scribal changes use `<subst>`.

answer.text: It flags a reading as uncertain so that a later editor can decide.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Uncertainty is `<unclear>`. `<choice>` holds alternatives that are both valid, for different purposes.

name.text: 05 Question: Short Forms and How to Record Them

questiontext.text: In `<expan>θε<ex>ό</ex>ς</expan>`, what is the `<ex>` tag doing?

generalfeedback.text: Encode the abbreviation and its expansion separately with `<ex>` marking supplied letters, so the model learns what is actually on the page.

answer.text: Marking the letters you supplied, which the scribe did not actually write.

feedback.text: Correct. It records exactly where the ink stops and your inference starts, and lets software italicize the supplied letters.

answer.text: Marking the letters that are hardest to read on the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Difficulty of reading is `<unclear>`. `<ex>` is about what is absent from the page altogether.

answer.text: Marking an example of the abbreviation for the training data.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is not an annotation for software; it is a statement about which characters are editorial.

answer.text: Marking letters that were once there but have since been lost to damage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lost material is `<gap/>` or `<supplied>`. `<ex>` concerns letters the scribe never wrote, because the word was shortened.

name.text: 06 Question: Saying What You Cannot Read

questiontext.text: What is the difference between `<unclear>` and `<gap/>`, and why does it matter?

generalfeedback.text: `<unclear>` proposes a reading with reduced confidence and `<gap/>` proposes nothing — conflating them misrepresents inference as absence or difficulty as loss.

answer.text: `<unclear>` contains a reading you are offering with reduced confidence; `<gap/>` is empty and offers nothing at all.

feedback.text: Correct. Putting a guess inside a `<gap/>` disguises inference as a hole in the page, and an empty `<unclear>` turns a hard reading into a loss.

answer.text: `<unclear>` is for faded ink and `<gap/>` is for water damage — they record different causes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cause is recorded by the `reason` attribute on either. The difference is whether you are offering a reading.

answer.text: `<unclear>` is used during transcription and `<gap/>` is added later by the editor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are used as you transcribe. They describe different situations, not different stages.

answer.text: They are interchangeable, so long as you use one of them consistently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They make opposite claims, and swapping them misrepresents your evidence.

name.text: 07 Question: When the Scribe Corrected Themselves

questiontext.text: A scribe crossed out a word and another person wrote a different one above it. Why record both rather than just the final wording?

generalfeedback.text: Scribal corrections are transmission evidence, and recording only the corrected text destroys it while leaving the reading unchanged.

answer.text: The correction is evidence about the manuscript's history and its relationship to other copies, and recording only the result destroys it.

feedback.text: Correct. In Week 7 a correction in one copy that matches another copy's original reading is exactly what links them.

answer.text: Because TEI requires every deletion to be preserved for the file to validate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema would accept the final wording alone. The reason is evidential, not technical.

answer.text: Because the crossed-out word is usually the correct reading and the correction is usually wrong.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neither is automatically right. What matters is that a change happened, in a direction, by somebody.

answer.text: Because software cannot process text that has had words removed from it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It processes it fine. The loss is scholarly, not computational.

name.text: 08 Question: Why Line Breaks Matter So Much Here

questiontext.text: Give one reason line breaks must be recorded in this transcription, when in an ordinary typed document they mean nothing.

generalfeedback.text: Line divisions are structural here — HTR trains on lines, your zones bind per line, and line breaks are codicological evidence.

answer.text: Tomorrow's software reads line by line, so its training examples have to be individual lines paired with their text.

feedback.text: Correct. A transcription without line divisions cannot train anything at all — and your image links from Lesson 3.3 are per line too.

answer.text: Because TEI files are invalid unless every line carries an `<lb/>` element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema does not require it. The requirement comes from what the lines are used for.

answer.text: Because line breaks are needed to make the transcription display correctly on a web page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Display is the least of it. They are needed for training, for image links, and as evidence about the scribe.

answer.text: Because the word count must match the manuscript exactly for scoring in Week 5.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scoring compares characters and words, not lines. The line divisions matter for training and for binding to the image.

name.text: 09 Question: Setting Up the File Before You Type

questiontext.text: Why check that your editor really saves UTF-8 and that the normalization hook works *before* you start typing Greek?

generalfeedback.text: Verify UTF-8, live schema validation, and the NFC hook before typing — a mixed-normalization ground truth invalidates Week 5.

answer.text: A character-encoding mismatch corrupts every Greek character, and accents stored two different ways make Week 5's scores meaningless.

feedback.text: Correct. Both are miserable to repair afterwards, and both are a two-minute check now.

answer.text: Because git refuses to commit files that are not UTF-8.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git will happily store the corrupted bytes. Nothing stops you — that is precisely the danger.

answer.text: Because Transkribus only accepts files that have passed a normalization check.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The problem appears much later, when scores are computed against a reference stored differently.

answer.text: Because polytonic Greek cannot be typed at all without the hook installed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You can type it perfectly well. The hook makes sure it is *stored* consistently.

name.text: 10 Question: How to Actually Do It

questiontext.text: Why is "type what you see, not what you expect" the rule that separates transcribing from reading?

generalfeedback.text: Type what you see rather than what you expect, and check your line position regularly — line skip silently invalidates every binding after it.

answer.text: If you know the passage, you will read the expected wording and never notice the difference — which is how genuine variants get erased.

feedback.text: Correct. It is the largest threat to your accuracy, and typing a difficult line backwards is a good defence against it.

answer.text: Because your memory of the text is probably of a different work altogether.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The danger is precisely that you remember the right work — the expectation is plausible, which is why it slips past.

answer.text: Because the software will later compare your text against the printed edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is compared against the image, through your transcription. The risk is to the evidence, not to a score.

answer.text: Because reading ahead is slower than transcribing one line at a time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reading ahead is faster, which is exactly why it is tempting and why it produces errors.

name.text: 11 Question: Getting to Know the Hand

questiontext.text: What is the point of spending fifteen minutes on `transcription/HAND.md` before transcribing in bulk?

generalfeedback.text: Characterize the hand before transcribing at volume, and record it — you will consult it on Wednesday to judge HTR errors.

answer.text: It disciplines your reading now, and tomorrow it tells you whether a software mistake is the program's fault or the scribe's.

feedback.text: Correct. It also documents your palaeographic reasoning for the Week 12 commentary.

answer.text: It is required documentation for submitting the manuscript to Transkribus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus asks for no such thing. The file is for you.

answer.text: It lets the software learn the letterforms before it sees any images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The software learns only from images paired with text. It never reads your notes.

answer.text: It records which letters to skip when they are too difficult to read.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Difficult letters get transcribed and marked, not skipped.

name.text: 12 Question: Accents and the Box Problem

questiontext.text: Why should you note how high above the line this scribe places the accents?

generalfeedback.text: Layout polygons drawn too tightly cut off Greek accents entirely, so note how high this hand places diacritics — you will adjust for it tomorrow.

answer.text: Tomorrow's software cuts a strip around each line, and if the strip is too tight the accents fall outside it and are never seen.

feedback.text: Correct. Your note tells you how far to widen the strips — which is Wednesday's first real task.

answer.text: Because accent height identifies the century in which the manuscript was copied.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It may be suggestive, but that is not why you are measuring it here.

answer.text: Because accents placed too high are usually later additions by a second hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Height is a feature of the scribe's habit, not evidence of a different writer.

answer.text: Because the software ignores accents entirely and you will have to add them by hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It reads them perfectly well — provided they are inside the strip it was given.

name.text: 13 Question: When There Are No Spaces Between Words

questiontext.text: Your manuscript runs its words together. What does this course recommend, and why?

generalfeedback.text: Supply word division and declare it in the header — and expect *scriptio continua* to make word error rate uninterpretable in Week 5.

answer.text: Put the spaces in, and state in your header that the spacing is yours and is not on the page.

feedback.text: Correct. The aim is not to avoid intervening — text with no spaces is nearly useless later — but to intervene openly.

answer.text: Reproduce it unspaced, since a diplomatic transcription must never add anything.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Faithful, but nearly unusable for comparing copies or looking up words — and the course prefers a declared intervention.

answer.text: Add the spaces silently, since word division is obvious to any competent reader.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is an unrecorded editorial act, which is exactly what a diplomatic transcription is meant to avoid.

answer.text: Record both versions with `<choice>`, since that is the only fully faithful option.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is faithful and it is legitimate, but it is extremely verbose — the course recommends the declared-spacing option.

name.text: 14 Question: Write Your Rules Down

questiontext.text: Why is being inconsistent worse than making any particular transcription choice?

generalfeedback.text: Write your conventions down and follow them — inconsistency is worse than any particular choice, for readers and for models alike.

answer.text: A reader cannot tell whether an unmarked instance means a different form or one you simply missed, so the whole record becomes uninterpretable.

feedback.text: Correct. And the software learns your inconsistency and reproduces it unpredictably.

answer.text: Because inconsistent files fail schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They validate perfectly. The damage is to interpretation, not to structure.

answer.text: Because the marking scheme penalizes inconsistency more heavily than wrong choices.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is about the scholarly usefulness of the result, not about marks.

answer.text: Because you will forget which convention you used and have to start over.

feedback.text: Incorrect — or at least, that is the smallest part of it. The real cost is that nobody can interpret the finished text.

name.text: 15 Question: How Accurate Is a Hand Transcription?

questiontext.text: What does double-keying do that simply proofreading once does not?

generalfeedback.text: Your ground truth will contain errors, which is why Week 5 double-keys it — transcribe now so that the second pass finds few differences.

answer.text: It produces two independent versions, so the places where they disagree pinpoint exactly where attention is needed.

feedback.text: Correct. Where two independent attempts agree, you are almost certainly right; where they differ is where to look.

answer.text: It doubles the amount of training data available for the software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The two versions describe the same lines — the gain is accuracy, not volume.

answer.text: It guarantees an error-free transcription, which is why Week 5 treats it as final.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is substantially better, not perfect. Week 5 still adjudicates the differences by hand.

answer.text: It removes the need to check the transcription against the images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjudicating a difference means going back to the image to settle it.

name.text: 16 Question: How Much to Get Done Today

questiontext.text: Why is one carefully transcribed page better than three rushed ones?

generalfeedback.text: One accurate folio beats three careless ones — today's conventions propagate into everything transcribed afterwards.

answer.text: Three sloppy pages are worse than nothing, because tomorrow the software learns your mistakes from them.

feedback.text: Correct. And today's habits set the conventions that every later page follows, so errors made now propagate.

answer.text: Because the software cannot accept more than one page of training data at a time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It takes as many as you give it. Quality, not quantity, is the constraint today.

answer.text: Because a single page is all that Week 5's measurement will use.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You will extend the transcription through the week. The point is that the first page must be right.

answer.text: Because marks are awarded for accuracy on one page rather than for coverage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is methodological — careless examples actively damage what you build next.

name.text: 17 Question: Which Pages to Pick Later

questiontext.text: Why is working straight through consecutive leaves the wrong way to choose training pages?

generalfeedback.text: Sample training pages across the corpus and deliberately include difficult ones, or the model will fail precisely where you need it.

answer.text: The program learns that one stretch of the book — its ink, its layout — and then stumbles on pages that differ.

feedback.text: Correct. Spreading your pages across the manuscript shows it the variety it will actually face.

answer.text: Because consecutive pages are usually by the same scribe, and variety of scribes is what matters most.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Even with one scribe throughout, ink, parchment, and layout vary across a book.

answer.text: Because the software processes pages in a random order anyway, so sequence is meaningless.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Order of processing is not the issue; what the examples collectively cover is.

answer.text: Because consecutive transcription takes longer than jumping between leaves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is generally quicker. The problem is what the resulting model can and cannot handle.

name.text: 18 Question: Checking Your Work Before You Save It

questiontext.text: Why count `<lb/>` elements against `<zone>` elements every session?

generalfeedback.text: Count `<lb/>` against `<zone>` every session — a mismatch means line skip, and every binding after it is wrong.

answer.text: If the counts differ you skipped or added a line, and every image link after that point is attached to the wrong strip.

feedback.text: Correct. The text still reads perfectly, so nothing else would reveal it.

answer.text: Because TEI requires the two counts to match for the file to validate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema does not check it. That is exactly why you have to.

answer.text: Because Transkribus rejects files whose line and zone counts disagree.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will import them and quietly mismatch your text to the wrong images.

answer.text: Because the counts are used to calculate the character error rate in Week 5.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The score compares text, not counts. This check catches a silent structural fault.

name.text: 19 Question: Saving It to Git Properly

questiontext.text: Why tag the transcription rather than just committing it?

generalfeedback.text: Tag the ground truth state, because Week 5's measurements are only reproducible against the exact version that was measured.

answer.text: Week 5 measures against this exact version, and a tag keeps that version retrievable even after you correct the file.

feedback.text: Correct. The old numbers stay meaningful and the correction shows up as a visible change.

answer.text: Because untagged commits are deleted automatically after a period of time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commits persist. A tag is a convenience for finding one again, not a protection against deletion.

answer.text: Because tagging is what marks the file as human-produced rather than machine-produced.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is what the `Human-Verified` and `AI-Generated` trailers do.

answer.text: Because Transkribus imports from tags rather than from the working files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus imports images from a web address and knows nothing about your tags.

name.text: 20 Question: What Rides on Getting This Right

questiontext.text: Why is a quietly tidied-up reference the most dangerous kind of error in this file?

generalfeedback.text: A silently normalized ground truth produces a model that modernizes invisibly — and standard error metrics will not detect it.

answer.text: The resulting output is clean and readable, so nothing signals that the historical spelling has been overwritten — and the usual scores will not detect it.

feedback.text: Correct. A program can post a low error rate while systematically destroying the old orthography.

answer.text: Because tidied text cannot be compared against machine output at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It compares perfectly well. That is the problem — the comparison looks fine and means the wrong thing.

answer.text: Because tidying introduces character-encoding errors that inflate the score.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a separate fault. Tidying is dangerous precisely because it does *not* inflate the score.

answer.text: Because tidied text takes longer to produce than a faithful transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is usually quicker, which is part of the temptation.

name.text: 21 Question: Why the Human Stays in the Loop

questiontext.text: Why can the order of the three-step cycle not be reversed?

generalfeedback.text: Correcting a machine transcription tests plausibility; transcribing independently tests correctness, and only the second gives you grounds for judgement.

answer.text: Somebody who starts from machine output and corrects it has never read the page alone, so they can only judge whether a reading looks plausible.

feedback.text: Correct. Judging plausibility is a much weaker test than working out what is actually there.

answer.text: Because the software needs the manual transcription as input before it can run at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It runs on images without any transcription. The manual step is needed for training and for measurement.

answer.text: Because the AI step on Friday would overwrite Wednesday's model if it ran first.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are independent runs. The reason is about the quality of human judgement.

answer.text: Because marks are awarded in sequence and the assignments must be submitted in order.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The sequence is methodological, not administrative.

name.text: 22 Question: What to Bring Tomorrow

questiontext.text: Why does your note on accent height matter for tomorrow specifically?

generalfeedback.text: Bring a validated, tagged transcription and a note of this hand's diacritic height — polygon correction is Wednesday's first task.

answer.text: Wednesday's first task is widening the line strips so accents fall inside them, and the note tells you how far to widen.

feedback.text: Correct. Without it you are guessing at a setting that determines whether the model ever sees a breathing mark.

answer.text: Because Transkribus asks for the accent height when you create a collection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It asks for no such thing. The measurement informs a correction you make yourself.

answer.text: Because the accent height determines which base model you should start from.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Base model choice is about script, date, and language.

answer.text: Because you will be asked to type the accents again at a different size.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You will not retype anything — you will adjust the boundaries of the strips.

name.text: 23 Question: Friday Is Remote

questiontext.text: Which item on the Friday checklist most often catches people out, and why?

generalfeedback.text: Test your full toolchain on the machine you will use Friday — push your repository, publish your manifest, install your keyboard.

answer.text: The Greek keyboard — a layout installed on a lab machine is not installed on your own laptop.

feedback.text: Correct. Discovering that on Friday morning costs you the session, and installing it today takes two minutes.

answer.text: The repository push, because pushing from off campus requires a different login.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The login is the same. Forgetting to push at all is the risk, not the network.

answer.text: The XML editor, because most editors will not run outside the university network.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They run fine offline. The schema must be reachable, which is worth checking, but the keyboard is the classic trap.

answer.text: The Transkribus credits, because they are only issued to on-campus machines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Credits are tied to the class allowance, not to a location.

name.text: 24 Question: Studying Your Own Mistakes

questiontext.text: Why record the *patterns* in your errors rather than just fixing the individual slips?

generalfeedback.text: Record the patterns in your own errors, because in Week 5 they tell you when to suspect yourself rather than the machine.

answer.text: In Week 5 they tell you when to suspect yourself rather than the machine.

feedback.text: Correct. Knowing you regularly confuse two letters in this hand is what lets you spot the cases where the machine is right and you are not.

answer.text: Because the patterns are submitted as part of the Transcription Assignment mark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They feed the reconciliation report, but the reason to record them is diagnostic.

answer.text: Because the software can be trained to avoid the same patterns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It learns from images and text, not from your notes about yourself.

answer.text: Because individual slips are usually not worth correcting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fix them all. The patterns are recorded *as well*, because they are informative in a way single errors are not.

name.text: 25 Question: Why Not Just Start with the Machine?

questiontext.text: What is the decisive argument against running the software first and correcting its output?

generalfeedback.text: Correcting machine output tests plausibility and anchors your judgement, which is exactly the wrong test on the hard readings.

answer.text: Correcting only tests whether a reading is believable; typing it yourself tests whether it is correct, and a suggestion anchors your judgement.

feedback.text: Correct. The two tests diverge most on exactly the hard readings where it matters.

answer.text: Untrained software is too slow to be worth running before a model has been trained.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed is not the issue — it is fast. The practical argument is that bad output costs more to fix than to retype.

answer.text: The software cannot produce output at all without first being given a transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A general model produces output immediately. That it needs training data is a separate, weaker argument.

answer.text: Machine output cannot be committed to git with the correct provenance labels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It can, and Wednesday shows you how.

name.text: 26 Question: A Worked Example

questiontext.text: Beyond the words themselves, what does the worked example record that a tidied-up transcription would lose?

generalfeedback.text: The encoding records abbreviation, uncertainty, correction, and loss — all evidence that later weeks need and that a clean transcription discards.

answer.text: Short forms as written, a doubtful reading with its cause and source, a correction by a second hand, and a measured hole.

feedback.text: Correct. Every one of those is evidence a later week needs — Week 6 for the short forms, Week 7 for the correction, Weeks 8 and 12 for the doubt and the loss.

answer.text: The line numbering, which a tidied version would renumber from one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line numbering survives tidying easily. What is lost is the evidential markup.

answer.text: The Greek accents, which tidying always removes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tidying usually keeps accents — it may even add ones the scribe omitted. The losses are elsewhere.

answer.text: The file's character encoding, which changes when text is regularized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Encoding is unrelated to whether the text has been regularized.

name.text: 27 Question: Checklist Before You Leave

questiontext.text: Why finish and validate today rather than carrying unfinished work into Wednesday?

generalfeedback.text: Finish and validate before Wednesday — tomorrow's work builds directly on this file.

answer.text: Tomorrow's work builds directly on this file, so an unchecked transcription stops the session.

feedback.text: Correct. You cannot correct line strips or train anything against a file that is not finished and valid.

answer.text: Because the file is submitted for marking at the end of Tuesday.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Transcription Assignment is due 2 October, at the end of Week 5.

answer.text: Because git will not let you commit an invalid XML file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git stores whatever you give it. Validation is your responsibility.

answer.text: Because Transkribus validates the file on import and rejects invalid TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It imports images, not your TEI file. The dependency is on your own next steps.

name.text: 28 Question: Where This Leads

questiontext.text: Today's file plays four different roles across the next two weeks. Name them.

generalfeedback.text: Today's file serves as training data, comparison reference, verification object, and measurement reference — four roles, one artefact.

answer.text: Training examples on Wednesday, a comparison on Friday, the thing being checked in Week 5, and the answer key at the end of Week 5.

feedback.text: Correct. One file doing four jobs is why its quality spreads so far.

answer.text: A draft, a corrected version, a final version, and a submitted version.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are stages of one file, not different roles it plays for different purposes.

answer.text: Training data, a backup, a marking record, and an archive copy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Backup and archiving are not roles in the methodology.

answer.text: An answer key on Wednesday, training data on Friday, and a draft in Week 5.

feedback.text: Incorrect — the order is reversed. It is training data on Wednesday and the answer key at the end of Week 5.

name.text: 29 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: Which part of good transcription is described as both the hardest and the most telling?

generalfeedback.text: Marking uncertainty honestly is the hardest and most diagnostic part of good transcription — a confident guess destroys the record of what was actually legible.

answer.text: Marking doubt honestly, including where you would rather resolve it and move on.

feedback.text: Correct. An honest `<unclear>` is more useful to every later reader than a confident guess — it is the difference between recording evidence and announcing a conclusion.

answer.text: Keeping the line numbering consistent across every folio.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Necessary and worth checking, but mechanical rather than difficult.

answer.text: Encoding every abbreviation with the full `<choice>` structure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Laborious, but it is a rule you can simply follow. Admitting doubt is a judgement you must resist avoiding.

answer.text: Producing enough folios to train a usable model.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Anchor

questiontext.text: Why is the manual step described as unavoidable rather than merely traditional?

generalfeedback.text: Automation is always measured against a reference, and a reference cannot be produced by the thing it measures — which is why the manual step is irreducible rather than merely traditional.

answer.text: A ruler cannot be checked against itself, so a program's own output cannot show whether the program is right.

feedback.text: Correct. This is structural, not a shortcoming of current technology that a better model will one day fix.

answer.text: Because no software currently reaches an acceptable error rate on Greek manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Some do very well. Even a perfect program would still need an independent reference to be shown to be perfect.

answer.text: Because copyright rules require a human-produced transcription in a scholarly edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The argument is about measurement, not about rights.

answer.text: Because the manual step is the only one that produces valid TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Machine output can be encoded as valid TEI. The issue is what it can be measured against.
